cues.text: Welcome to Study Session Three of MIT 8107, Software Development Lifecycle.
This session is on Testing and Quality Assurance, and we begin with the first chapter: Testing and QA.
Let us start with the most basic question.
What is testing?
Testing evaluates software to discover defects and to provide evidence of quality.
Notice the two purposes there.
We test to find problems, and we also test to gather evidence about how good the software is.
Next, three terms that people often blur together.
Quality assurance, usually shortened to QA, is process-oriented.
Its focus is prevention and improvement: it looks at how we work, so that fewer problems arise in the first place.
Quality control, by contrast, evaluates the outputs of the product itself.
And testing is a major activity within quality control.
So testing sits inside quality control, while quality assurance is about the process that surrounds the work.
Now let us be precise about how things go wrong, because three words are used here with distinct meanings.
An error is a human mistake.
A defect is a flaw in the software.
And a failure is observable incorrect behaviour during execution.
You can think of it as a chain: a person makes an error, that error leaves a defect in the software, and when the software runs, that defect may show up as a failure that someone can actually see.
Another pair of ideas you must keep apart is verification and validation.
Verification asks whether the specified requirements are met.
Validation asks whether the software satisfies the actual needs.
So verification checks the software against what was written down, while validation checks it against what people really need.
Two cautions follow.
First, exhaustive testing is generally impossible.
We cannot try every input in every situation, so we must prioritise risk and evidence.
Second, passing tests do not prove the absence of defects.
A suite of passing tests tells you that those checks passed; it does not tell you that no defects remain.
Now let us look at the test levels.
Please refer to the table on your screen.
It has three columns: Test level, Scope, and Example.
There are four rows, and I will take them in order.
First row: the Unit level.
Its scope is a small function or class in isolation.
The example given is a shipping-cost function.
So you test that one function by itself.
Second row: the Integration level.
Its scope is the interfaces between components or services.
The example is an API writing the correct database record.
Here the question is whether the pieces work properly together at their boundaries.
Third row: the System level.
Its scope is the complete integrated system, tested against requirements.
The example is the full learning portal, including performance and security.
Fourth row: Acceptance, also called UAT, which stands for user acceptance testing.
Its scope is business and user readiness.
The example is staff validating admission workflows.
Notice how the scope grows as we move down the table, from a single function, to connections between parts, to the whole system, and finally to whether the business and users are ready to accept it.
Let us now turn to types of testing.
Functional testing checks behaviour, that is, what the software does.
Nonfunctional testing checks quality attributes, such as how well it does it.
Next, regression versus retesting.
Regression testing checks existing behaviour after changes, to make sure that something which worked before has not been broken.
Retesting, also called confirmation testing, verifies a specific fix, that is, it confirms that a particular reported problem is now resolved.
Then smoke versus sanity.
Smoke testing checks the critical functions of a build.
Sanity testing focuses on a limited change.
The source adds a qualification here: terminology varies.
So be aware that different teams may use these two terms differently.
Performance testing has several kinds.
Load testing uses expected traffic.
Stress testing goes beyond expected traffic.
Endurance testing, also called soak testing, runs over time.
Then there are spike testing and scalability testing.
Security testing assesses controls, and it must be done within an authorised scope.
Usability and accessibility testing check whether real users are able to complete tasks.
Compatibility testing covers devices, browsers and environments.
And recovery tests verify restore and failover.
Finally, let us look at different approaches to testing.
Black-box testing uses external specifications, without looking inside.
White-box testing uses the internal structure.
Grey-box testing combines the two, with limited internal knowledge.
Static analysis reviews code or design without executing it.
Dynamic testing, in contrast, executes the software.
Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution together.
Scripted testing follows predefined cases.
And last, risk-based testing focuses on likelihood and impact, on critical workflows, and on changes.
This connects back to what we said earlier: since we cannot test everything, we direct our effort where the risk is greatest.
